fp1_matrices_operations.description: Add conformable matrices, use row-by-column multiplication and compare the dimensions and order of products.

sections.title: When can two matrices be added or subtracted?
sections.label: Match row and column positions
sections.intro: Both matrices must have the same number of rows and columns. A scalar multiplier changes every entry, without changing dimensions.

blocks.html: Do the scalar multiplications first, then combine corresponding entries. The zero matrix leaves any same-sized matrix unchanged under addition.

blocks.title: Add and subtract entries in matching positions
blocks.prompt: Let \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & -2\\3 & 3\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}0 & 3\\-1 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find all entries of \(2A-B\).
blocks.hint: Matrix subtraction acts entry by entry after matching dimensions.
blocks.solution:
Both matrices have two rows and two columns. Double every entry of A first.

Subtract the entry of B at the same row and column. For example the top-right entry is \(2(-2)-3=-7\).

The resulting matrix is \(\left[\begin{matrix}4 & -7\\7 & 5\end{matrix}\right]\).

blocks.html: Matrix addition does not mix rows or columns. Subtract only the matching entry.

sections.title: Which dimensions determine whether a product exists?
sections.label: Match the inner dimensions
sections.intro: A row of the first matrix and a column of the second must contain the same number of entries for their dot product.

blocks.html: An \(m\times p\) matrix multiplied by a \(p\times n\) matrix gives an \(m\times n\) matrix.

blocks.title: Multiply a rectangular matrix row by column
blocks.prompt: Calculate \(AB\) for \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & -1 & 2\\0 & 3 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 2\\-1 & 2\\2 & 0\end{matrix}\right]\).
blocks.hint: Each answer uses one row of the first matrix and one column of the second.
blocks.solution:
A has three columns and B has three rows. The inner dimensions agree, leaving two rows and two columns.

For the top-right entry use the first row of A and second column of B. The sum of their products is \(2\).

Doing this for the remaining entries gives \(\left[\begin{matrix}7 & 2\\-1 & 6\end{matrix}\right]\).

blocks.html: The matching inner dimension controls the multiplication sum. The remaining outer dimensions control the shape.

sections.title: Why can reversing the order change the answer?
sections.label: Compare rows with columns in the stated order
sections.intro: A product specifies which matrix supplies rows. Reversing factors changes all those pairings, and it may even make the product undefined.

blocks.html: Compare the two products entry by entry if both exist. One differing entry is sufficient to prove the matrices differ.

blocks.title: Compare multiplication in the opposite order
blocks.prompt: For \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & -2\\3 & 3\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}0 & 3\\-1 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\), give the top-left entry of \(AB\) and of \(BA\).
blocks.hint: Changing the order changes which numbers form each dot product.
blocks.solution:
For AB use the first row of A against the first column of B. The result is \(2\).

For BA the roles switch. Use the first row of B against the first column of A for \(9\).

The entries differ for this choice, so the two whole products are unequal.

blocks.html: Ordinary scalar multiplication commutes, but you cannot assume that for a matrix product.

blocks.title: Compare multiplication in the opposite order
blocks.prompt: For \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & -2\\3 & 5\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}0 & 5\\-1 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\), give the top-left entry of \(AB\) and of \(BA\).
blocks.hint: Changing the order changes which numbers form each dot product.
blocks.solution:
For AB use the first row of A against the first column of B. The result is \(2\).

For BA the roles switch. Use the first row of B against the first column of A for \(15\).

The entries differ for this choice, so the two whole products are unequal.

sections.title: How large should an identity matrix be?
sections.label: Match the side of multiplication
sections.intro: An identity has ones along the leading diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Its size is chosen so that the multiplication exists.

blocks.html: For an \(m\times n\) matrix A, \(I_mA=A\) and \(AI_n=A\).

blocks.title: Choose the identity of the correct size
blocks.prompt: The matrix \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1 & 0\\-1 & 4 & 2\end{matrix}\right]\) is multiplied on the right by an identity matrix. Give the dimension of that identity, and give the entry in row two, column three of the product.

fields.label: Number of rows of the identity

blocks.hint: The identity leaves the matrix unchanged, but its size depends on the side of multiplication.
blocks.solution:
To multiply on the right of a matrix with three columns, use an identity of size three.

Its third column is \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\0\\1\end{matrix}\right]\). The dot product with the second row picks out its third entry.

So the product is the original matrix and the requested entry is \(2\).

blocks.html: A rectangular matrix may need two different identity sizes on the two sides.

sections.title: How do I recover the unknown column in a product?
sections.label: Write one equation per row
sections.intro: Equating a matrix–column product to a given output gives one scalar equation for each row.

blocks.html: Expand the row products, solve the simultaneous equations and substitute the recovered coordinates into the original matrix product.

blocks.title: Read a product as two simultaneous equations
blocks.prompt: Let \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & -2\\3 & 3\end{matrix}\right]\). The product with column \(\left[\begin{matrix}x\\y\end{matrix}\right]\) is \(\left[\begin{matrix}6\\9\end{matrix}\right]\). Find \(x,y\).
blocks.hint: Use one equation for each row instead of treating the column as a scalar.
blocks.solution:
Equate the first and second row products to the corresponding target entries.

Eliminate one variable from the two equations. This gives \(x=3\) and \(y=0\).

Check by multiplying A by the recovered column. The product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}6\\9\end{matrix}\right]\).

blocks.html: Do not divide by a matrix as if it were a scalar. The equations or a suitable inverse give the solution.

blocks.title: Read a product as two simultaneous equations
blocks.prompt: Let \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & -2\\3 & 5\end{matrix}\right]\). The product with column \(\left[\begin{matrix}x\\y\end{matrix}\right]\) is \(\left[\begin{matrix}16\\25\end{matrix}\right]\). Find \(x,y\).
blocks.hint: Use one equation for each row instead of treating the column as a scalar.
blocks.solution:
Equate the first and second row products to the corresponding target entries.

Eliminate one variable from the two equations. This gives \(x=5\) and \(y=2\).

Check by multiplying A by the recovered column. The product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}16\\25\end{matrix}\right]\).

solution: A has three columns and B has three rows. The inner dimensions agree, leaving two rows and two columns.

For BA the roles switch. Use the first row of B against the first column of A for \(6\).
The entries differ for this choice, so the two whole products are unequal.

examples.question: The matrix \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 1 & 0\\-1 & 3 & 2\end{matrix}\right]\) is multiplied on the right by an identity matrix. Give the dimension of that identity, and give the entry in row two, column three of the product.

solution: Equate the first and second row products to the corresponding target entries.
Eliminate one variable from the two equations. This gives \(x=2\) and \(y=-1\).
Check by multiplying A by the recovered column. The product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}4\\4\end{matrix}\right]\).

Check by multiplying A by the recovered column. The product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}10\\16\end{matrix}\right]\).

fp1_matrices_inverses.description: Find two- and three-dimensional matrix inverses and undo products on the correct side, including composite inverses.

sections.title: What makes a two-by-two matrix invertible?
sections.label: Check determinant before inverting
sections.intro: The inverse exists only for a non-zero determinant and must give the identity when multiplied on either side of the original matrix.

blocks.html: For a two-by-two matrix, swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal entries and divide by the determinant.

blocks.title: Compute an inverse by its determinant and four entries
blocks.prompt: Find the inverse of \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1\\3 & 5\end{matrix}\right]\).
blocks.hint: The determinant divides every entry, including the off-diagonal ones.
blocks.solution:
The determinant is \(12\), which is non-zero.

Swap the diagonal entries and negate the two off-diagonal entries to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}5 & -1\\-3 & 3\end{matrix}\right]\).

Divide each entry by the determinant. The inverse is \(\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{5}{12} & - \frac{1}{12}\\- \frac{1}{4} & \frac{1}{4}\end{matrix}\right]\).

blocks.html: Apply the determinant divisor to all four entries. A zero determinant means there is no inverse.

sections.title: How can I build the inverse of a three-by-three matrix?
sections.label: Solve for each unit image
sections.intro: The jth column of the inverse must be mapped by A to the jth column of the identity. Solve those systems separately when the structure makes this efficient.

blocks.html: For a triangular matrix, solve from the bottom upward if it is upper triangular. For a general invertible matrix, the cofactor matrix transposed and divided by the determinant also gives the inverse.

blocks.title: Find a triangular inverse by solving three columns
blocks.prompt: Find the inverse of \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 3 & 2\\0 & 1 & 2\\0 & 0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\).
blocks.hint: Each column of the inverse must map to its matching unit column under A.
blocks.solution:
The diagonal product gives determinant one. The columns of the inverse solve \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{e}_j\) for each unit column.

For the third column solve from the bottom upward. This gives \(\left[\begin{matrix}4\\-2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\).

Do the same for the first two unit columns to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}1 & -3 & 4\\0 & 1 & -2\\0 & 0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Verify by multiplication.

blocks.html: In the cofactor method, transpose before dividing. In the column method, put each solution in its own column.

sections.title: Which side undoes a left multiplier?
sections.label: Use the cancellation next to A
sections.intro: The order of factors prevents moving an inverse freely across other matrices. For a left multiplier, place the inverse in front of the full equation.

blocks.html: \(AX=C\) gives \(X=A^{-1}C\) when A is invertible.

blocks.title: Remove a left multiplier on the left
blocks.prompt: Given \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1\\3 & 5\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}5 & 10\\1 & 26\end{matrix}\right]\), solve \(AX=C\) for \(X\).
blocks.hint: Place the inverse next to the factor it cancels, on the same side of both products.
blocks.solution:
The determinant of A is non-zero. Multiply the whole equation by the inverse of A on the left.

The inverse and A cancel as adjacent factors. This gives \(X=A^{-1}C\).

Compute that product to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 2\\-1 & 4\end{matrix}\right]\).

blocks.html: Reversing the order of the solution generally gives a different result.

blocks.title: Remove a left multiplier on the left
blocks.prompt: Given \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}5 & 1\\3 & 7\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}19 & 16\\5 & 48\end{matrix}\right]\), solve \(AX=C\) for \(X\).
blocks.hint: Place the inverse next to the factor it cancels, on the same side of both products.
blocks.solution:
The determinant of A is non-zero. Multiply the whole equation by the inverse of A on the left.

The inverse and A cancel as adjacent factors. This gives \(X=A^{-1}C\).

Compute that product to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 2\\-1 & 6\end{matrix}\right]\).

sections.title: What changes for a right multiplier?
sections.label: Apply the inverse on the right
sections.intro: Keep a right multiplier on the right when undoing it. The inverse needs to meet the factor it cancels.

blocks.html: \(XA=C\) gives \(X=CA^{-1}\) for invertible A.

blocks.title: Remove a right multiplier on the right
blocks.prompt: Given \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1\\3 & 5\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & -3\\21 & 15\end{matrix}\right]\), solve \(XA=C\) for \(X\).
blocks.hint: Do not put the inverse on the left merely because it appears first in another example.
blocks.solution:
Here A acts on the right of X, so multiply by its inverse from the right.

This gives \(X=CA^{-1}\).

The resulting product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}2 & -1\\5 & 2\end{matrix}\right]\). Multiplying it by A from the right returns C.

blocks.html: Applying the inverse on the opposite side does not put it beside the factor to be removed.

sections.title: Why is a composite inverse reversed?
sections.label: Undo the most recent map first
sections.intro: The most recent operation must be undone before the previous one. In matrix multiplication this appears as a reversal of the factor order.

blocks.html: \((ABC)^{-1}=C^{-1}B^{-1}A^{-1}\) when every factor is invertible. Verify by cancelling adjacent inverse factors in the product.

blocks.title: Reverse the order of three factors
blocks.prompt: Let \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1\\3 & 5\end{matrix}\right]\), \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 3\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0\\2 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the determinant and top-left entry of \((ABC)^{-1}\).
blocks.hint: Reverse the factor order, keeping the individual inverse of each factor.
blocks.solution:
Undo the three maps in reverse order: \((ABC)^{-1}=C^{-1}B^{-1}A^{-1}\).

Multiply the three inverses in that order. The product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{7}{6} & - \frac{5}{6}\\- \frac{31}{12} & \frac{23}{12}\end{matrix}\right]\).

Its determinant is the reciprocal of \((\det A)(\det B)(\det C)\), giving \(\frac{1}{12}\).

blocks.html: Keep inverse and transpose rules separate. Both reverse products, but they act differently on each matrix.

blocks.title: Reverse the order of three factors
blocks.prompt: Let \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}5 & 1\\3 & 7\end{matrix}\right]\), \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 5\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0\\4 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the determinant and top-left entry of \((ABC)^{-1}\).
blocks.hint: Reverse the factor order, keeping the individual inverse of each factor.
blocks.solution:
Undo the three maps in reverse order: \((ABC)^{-1}=C^{-1}B^{-1}A^{-1}\).

Multiply the three inverses in that order. The product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{11}{16} & - \frac{13}{16}\\- \frac{91}{32} & \frac{109}{32}\end{matrix}\right]\).

Its determinant is the reciprocal of \((\det A)(\det B)(\det C)\), giving \(\frac{1}{32}\).

examples.title: Compute an inverse by its determinant and four entries
examples.question: Find the inverse of \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 1\\3 & 4\end{matrix}\right]\).
solution: The determinant is \(5\), which is non-zero.
Swap the diagonal entries and negate the two off-diagonal entries to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}4 & -1\\-3 & 2\end{matrix}\right]\).
Divide each entry by the determinant. The inverse is \(\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{4}{5} & - \frac{1}{5}\\- \frac{3}{5} & \frac{2}{5}\end{matrix}\right]\).

examples.title: Find a triangular inverse by solving three columns
examples.question: Find the inverse of \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 2 & 2\\0 & 1 & 1\\0 & 0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\).
solution: The diagonal product gives determinant one. The columns of the inverse solve \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{e}_j\) for each unit column.
For the third column solve from the bottom upward. This gives \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\-1\\1\end{matrix}\right]\).
Do the same for the first two unit columns to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}1 & -2 & 0\\0 & 1 & -1\\0 & 0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Verify by multiplication.

examples.title: Remove a left multiplier on the left
examples.question: Given \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 1\\3 & 4\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 7\\-1 & 18\end{matrix}\right]\), solve \(AX=C\) for \(X\).
solution: The determinant of A is non-zero. Multiply the whole equation by the inverse of A on the left.
The inverse and A cancel as adjacent factors. This gives \(X=A^{-1}C\).
Compute that product to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 2\\-1 & 3\end{matrix}\right]\).

examples.title: Remove a left multiplier on the left
examples.question: Given \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 1\\3 & 6\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}11 & 13\\3 & 36\end{matrix}\right]\), solve \(AX=C\) for \(X\).
solution: The determinant of A is non-zero. Multiply the whole equation by the inverse of A on the left.
The inverse and A cancel as adjacent factors. This gives \(X=A^{-1}C\).
Compute that product to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 2\\-1 & 5\end{matrix}\right]\).

examples.title: Remove a right multiplier on the right
examples.question: Given \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 1\\3 & 4\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & -2\\14 & 12\end{matrix}\right]\), solve \(XA=C\) for \(X\).
solution: Here A acts on the right of X, so multiply by its inverse from the right.
This gives \(X=CA^{-1}\).
The resulting product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}2 & -1\\4 & 2\end{matrix}\right]\). Multiplying it by A from the right returns C.

examples.title: Reverse the order of three factors
examples.question: Let \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 1\\3 & 4\end{matrix}\right]\), \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 2\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0\\1 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the determinant and top-left entry of \((ABC)^{-1}\).
solution: Undo the three maps in reverse order: \((ABC)^{-1}=C^{-1}B^{-1}A^{-1}\).
Multiply the three inverses in that order. The product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}2 & -1\\- \frac{13}{5} & \frac{7}{5}\end{matrix}\right]\).
Its determinant is the reciprocal of \((\det A)(\det B)(\det C)\), giving \(\frac{1}{5}\).

examples.title: Reverse the order of three factors
examples.question: Let \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 1\\3 & 6\end{matrix}\right]\), \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 4\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0\\3 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the determinant and top-left entry of \((ABC)^{-1}\).
solution: Undo the three maps in reverse order: \((ABC)^{-1}=C^{-1}B^{-1}A^{-1}\).
Multiply the three inverses in that order. The product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{6}{7} & - \frac{17}{21}\\- \frac{19}{7} & \frac{55}{21}\end{matrix}\right]\).
Its determinant is the reciprocal of \((\det A)(\det B)(\det C)\), giving \(\frac{1}{21}\).

extraPractice.title: Compute an inverse by its determinant and four entries

extraPractice.hint: Each column of the inverse must map to its matching unit column under A.

Do the same for the first two unit columns to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}1 & -4 & 10\\0 & 1 & -3\\0 & 0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Verify by multiplication.

extraPractice.title: Remove a left multiplier on the left
extraPractice.prompt: Given \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}6 & 1\\3 & 8\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}29 & 19\\7 & 62\end{matrix}\right]\), solve \(AX=C\) for \(X\).
extraPractice.hint: Place the inverse next to the factor it cancels, on the same side of both products.
extraPractice.solution:
The determinant of A is non-zero. Multiply the whole equation by the inverse of A on the left.

The inverse and A cancel as adjacent factors. This gives \(X=A^{-1}C\).

Compute that product to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}5 & 2\\-1 & 7\end{matrix}\right]\).

extraPractice.title: Remove a right multiplier on the right
extraPractice.prompt: Given \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 1\\3 & 6\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}5 & -4\\30 & 18\end{matrix}\right]\), solve \(XA=C\) for \(X\).
extraPractice.hint: Do not put the inverse on the left merely because it appears first in another example.
extraPractice.solution:
Here A acts on the right of X, so multiply by its inverse from the right.

This gives \(X=CA^{-1}\).

The resulting product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}2 & -1\\6 & 2\end{matrix}\right]\). Multiplying it by A from the right returns C.

extraPractice.title: Reverse the order of three factors
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}6 & 1\\3 & 8\end{matrix}\right]\), \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 6\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(C=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0\\5 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the determinant and top-left entry of \((ABC)^{-1}\).
extraPractice.hint: Reverse the factor order, keeping the individual inverse of each factor.
extraPractice.solution:
Undo the three maps in reverse order: \((ABC)^{-1}=C^{-1}B^{-1}A^{-1}\).

Multiply the three inverses in that order. The product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{26}{45} & - \frac{37}{45}\\- \frac{133}{45} & \frac{191}{45}\end{matrix}\right]\).

Its determinant is the reciprocal of \((\det A)(\det B)(\det C)\), giving \(\frac{1}{45}\).

glossary.definition: Matrix that multiplies the original to the identity.
A square matrix whose determinant is non-zero.
A square matrix with determinant zero.
A minor determinant with its alternating position sign.
Transpose of the cofactor matrix.

revision.body:
Choose the next step

SituationMethod
Two by twoSwap diagonals, negate off-diagonals and divide by the determinant.
Three by threeUse the adjugate formula or solve each unit-column equation.
Left multiplier\(AX=C\Rightarrow X=A^{-1}C\).
Composite inverseReverse the order and invert every factor.

Try a quick check

If \(A,B\) are invertible and \(ABX=I\), find \(X\).

Check \(X=B^{-1}A^{-1}\).
revision.checks:
• Apply the determinant divisor to all four entries. A zero determinant means there is no inverse.
  • In the cofactor method, transpose before dividing. In the column method, put each solution in its own column.
revision.examTip: Check an inverse by multiplying to the identity. For an equation, substitute the candidate on the original side.

fp1_matrices_determinants.description: Evaluate determinants using cofactors and row operations, find singular cases and interpret orientation, area and volume.

sections.title: How does a determinant locate a singular parameter?
sections.label: Set the determinant to zero
sections.intro: A determinant assigns a signed number to a square matrix. A non-zero result certifies that the map is invertible.

blocks.html: For a two-by-two matrix with entries \(a,b,c,d\) in row order, the determinant is \(ad-bc\). Set it to zero to find singular cases.

blocks.title: Identify the unique singular parameter
blocks.prompt: Find the value of \(k\) for which \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 4\\k & 2\end{matrix}\right]\) is singular. Find the determinant when \(k=0\).
blocks.hint: Set the determinant, not an individual entry, equal to zero.
blocks.solution:
The determinant is \(6 - 4 k\). A matrix is singular if and only if its determinant is zero.

Solve this linear equation to get \(k=\frac{3}{2}\).

For zero k the determinant is \(6\).

blocks.html: A zero entry alone does not imply the determinant is zero.

sections.title: Which row makes a three-by-three determinant simplest?
sections.label: Expand along a sparse row or column
sections.intro: A cofactor is the determinant of the smaller matrix left by removing one row and column, with a position-dependent sign.

blocks.html: Multiply each chosen-row entry by its cofactor and add the results. A zero entry contributes nothing.

blocks.title: Choose a sparse row for a cofactor expansion
blocks.prompt: Find the determinant of \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1 & -2\\0 & 4 & 0\\1 & -1 & 2\end{matrix}\right]\). Give the determinant of the minor obtained by deleting the second row and second column as well.
blocks.hint: The middle entry’s sign is positive because row plus column is even.
blocks.solution:
The second row contains two zeros, leaving one term.

The centre entry has positive cofactor sign. The minor determinant is \(8\).

Multiplying by the centre entry gives \(\det A=32\).

blocks.html: The cofactor signs alternate across each row and column. They do not depend on the actual entry values.

sections.title: What happens after a row operation?
sections.label: Track swaps, additions and scaling
sections.intro: A row swap changes the determinant’s sign. Scaling one row scales the determinant by that factor. Adding a multiple of another row leaves it unchanged.

blocks.html: Keep a running multiplier or sign each time you simplify a matrix before expanding.

blocks.title: Track the effect of two row operations on a determinant
blocks.prompt: Begin with \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1\\-1 & 4\end{matrix}\right]\). Swap rows one and two. Then add \(3\) times the first row of the new matrix to its second row. Find the determinant after each step.
blocks.hint: Keep track of whether an operation swaps, scales or adds rows.
blocks.solution:
The original determinant is \(13\). Swapping reverses the sign to \(-13\).

Adding a multiple of one row to another does not change the determinant.

The determinant after both operations is therefore \(-13\).

blocks.html: A row operation need not preserve the determinant. Only addition of a multiple of a different row does so without adjustment.

blocks.title: Track the effect of two row operations on a determinant
blocks.prompt: Begin with \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}5 & 1\\-1 & 6\end{matrix}\right]\). Swap rows one and two. Then add \(5\) times the first row of the new matrix to its second row. Find the determinant after each step.
blocks.hint: Keep track of whether an operation swaps, scales or adds rows.
blocks.solution:
The original determinant is \(31\). Swapping reverses the sign to \(-31\).

Adding a multiple of one row to another does not change the determinant.

The determinant after both operations is therefore \(-31\).

sections.title: Why does an area scale use the magnitude?
sections.label: Separate orientation and size
sections.intro: The determinant’s sign records whether a plane transformation reverses orientation. Its magnitude measures area scale.

blocks.html: Multiply the starting area by \(|\det A|\). A negative determinant reverses orientation but cannot make the area negative.

blocks.title: Distinguish orientation from a positive area scale
blocks.prompt: A plane transformation uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1\\1 & -3\end{matrix}\right]\). A region has area \(6\). Give the area of its image and state whether orientation is preserved.
blocks.hint: An area is positive even when the transformation reverses orientation.
blocks.solution:
The determinant is \(-10\), so the orientation reverses.

Use the absolute determinant as the area scale. It is \(10\).

The image area is \(60\).

blocks.html: Do not apply a one-coordinate stretch factor to an arbitrary two-dimensional area calculation.

sections.title: What does a three-dimensional determinant measure?
sections.label: Use the magnitude for volume
sections.intro: A linear transformation in three dimensions scales volumes by the magnitude of its determinant. The sign describes orientation.

blocks.html: For a triangular matrix compute the determinant from its diagonal product. Then use its absolute value for the scale.

blocks.title: Use a three-dimensional determinant to scale volume
blocks.prompt: A transformation uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 0 & 1\\0 & 2 & 1\\0 & 0 & -1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find its volume scale factor and the image volume of a solid with volume \(5\).
blocks.hint: The off-diagonal entries can shear a solid without changing the volume factor.
blocks.solution:
The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product on its diagonal. Here it is \(-6\).

The volume scale factor is its magnitude, \(6\).

The resulting volume is \(30\).

blocks.html: Upper-triangular off-diagonal entries may change a shape while leaving the determinant at its diagonal product.

blocks.title: Use a three-dimensional determinant to scale volume
blocks.prompt: A transformation uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}5 & 0 & 1\\0 & 2 & 1\\0 & 0 & -1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find its volume scale factor and the image volume of a solid with volume \(7\).
blocks.hint: The off-diagonal entries can shear a solid without changing the volume factor.
blocks.solution:
The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product on its diagonal. Here it is \(-10\).

The volume scale factor is its magnitude, \(10\).

The resulting volume is \(70\).

examples.title: Identify the unique singular parameter
examples.question: Find the value of \(k\) for which \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 3\\k & 1\end{matrix}\right]\) is singular. Find the determinant when \(k=0\).
solution: The determinant is \(2 - 3 k\). A matrix is singular if and only if its determinant is zero.
Solve this linear equation to get \(k=\frac{2}{3}\).
For zero k the determinant is \(2\).

examples.title: Choose a sparse row for a cofactor expansion
examples.question: Find the determinant of \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 1 & -2\\0 & 3 & 0\\1 & -1 & 2\end{matrix}\right]\). Give the determinant of the minor obtained by deleting the second row and second column as well.
solution: The second row contains two zeros, leaving one term.
The centre entry has positive cofactor sign. The minor determinant is \(6\).
Multiplying by the centre entry gives \(\det A=18\).

examples.title: Track the effect of two row operations on a determinant
examples.question: Begin with \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 1\\-1 & 3\end{matrix}\right]\). Swap rows one and two. Then add \(2\) times the first row of the new matrix to its second row. Find the determinant after each step.
solution: The original determinant is \(7\). Swapping reverses the sign to \(-7\).
Adding a multiple of one row to another does not change the determinant.
The determinant after both operations is therefore \(-7\).

examples.title: Track the effect of two row operations on a determinant
examples.question: Begin with \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 1\\-1 & 5\end{matrix}\right]\). Swap rows one and two. Then add \(4\) times the first row of the new matrix to its second row. Find the determinant after each step.
solution: The original determinant is \(21\). Swapping reverses the sign to \(-21\).
Adding a multiple of one row to another does not change the determinant.
The determinant after both operations is therefore \(-21\).

examples.title: Distinguish orientation from a positive area scale
examples.question: A plane transformation uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 1\\1 & -2\end{matrix}\right]\). A region has area \(5\). Give the area of its image and state whether orientation is preserved.
solution: The determinant is \(-5\), so the orientation reverses.
Use the absolute determinant as the area scale. It is \(5\).
The image area is \(25\).

examples.title: Use a three-dimensional determinant to scale volume
examples.question: A transformation uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 0 & 1\\0 & 2 & 1\\0 & 0 & -1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find its volume scale factor and the image volume of a solid with volume \(4\).
solution: The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product on its diagonal. Here it is \(-4\).
The volume scale factor is its magnitude, \(4\).
The resulting volume is \(16\).

examples.title: Use a three-dimensional determinant to scale volume
examples.question: A transformation uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 0 & 1\\0 & 2 & 1\\0 & 0 & -1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find its volume scale factor and the image volume of a solid with volume \(6\).
solution: The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product on its diagonal. Here it is \(-8\).
The volume scale factor is its magnitude, \(8\).
The resulting volume is \(48\).

extraPractice.title: Identify the unique singular parameter
extraPractice.prompt: Find the value of \(k\) for which \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 5\\k & 3\end{matrix}\right]\) is singular. Find the determinant when \(k=0\).
extraPractice.hint: Set the determinant, not an individual entry, equal to zero.
extraPractice.solution:
The determinant is \(12 - 5 k\). A matrix is singular if and only if its determinant is zero.

Solve this linear equation to get \(k=\frac{12}{5}\).

For zero k the determinant is \(12\).

extraPractice.title: Choose a sparse row for a cofactor expansion
extraPractice.prompt: Find the determinant of \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 1 & -2\\0 & 5 & 0\\1 & -1 & 2\end{matrix}\right]\). Give the determinant of the minor obtained by deleting the second row and second column as well.
extraPractice.hint: The middle entry’s sign is positive because row plus column is even.
extraPractice.solution:
The second row contains two zeros, leaving one term.

The centre entry has positive cofactor sign. The minor determinant is \(10\).

Multiplying by the centre entry gives \(\det A=50\).

extraPractice.title: Track the effect of two row operations on a determinant
extraPractice.prompt: Begin with \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}6 & 1\\-1 & 7\end{matrix}\right]\). Swap rows one and two. Then add \(6\) times the first row of the new matrix to its second row. Find the determinant after each step.
extraPractice.hint: Keep track of whether an operation swaps, scales or adds rows.
extraPractice.solution:
The original determinant is \(43\). Swapping reverses the sign to \(-43\).

Adding a multiple of one row to another does not change the determinant.

The determinant after both operations is therefore \(-43\).

extraPractice.title: Distinguish orientation from a positive area scale
extraPractice.prompt: A plane transformation uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 1\\1 & -4\end{matrix}\right]\). A region has area \(7\). Give the area of its image and state whether orientation is preserved.
extraPractice.hint: An area is positive even when the transformation reverses orientation.
extraPractice.solution:
The determinant is \(-17\), so the orientation reverses.

Use the absolute determinant as the area scale. It is \(17\).

The image area is \(119\).

extraPractice.title: Use a three-dimensional determinant to scale volume
extraPractice.prompt: A transformation uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}6 & 0 & 1\\0 & 2 & 1\\0 & 0 & -1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find its volume scale factor and the image volume of a solid with volume \(8\).
extraPractice.hint: The off-diagonal entries can shear a solid without changing the volume factor.
extraPractice.solution:
The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product on its diagonal. Here it is \(-12\).

The volume scale factor is its magnitude, \(12\).

The resulting volume is \(96\).

glossary.definition: Signed scale associated with a square matrix.
Determinant after deleting one row and column.
Positive or negative sign attached to a position in a determinant expansion.
Order of a frame of directions, possibly reversed by a map.
Positive magnitude multiplying an area or volume.

Try a quick check

A transformation has determinant \(-3\). What happens to an area of \(5\)?

Check Its image has area \(15\) and reversed orientation.

  • The cofactor signs alternate across each row and column. They do not depend on the actual entry values.

fp1_matrices_plane_maps.description: Build plane matrices from unit images, compose transformations in order, recover a map and transform a line.

sections.title: How do the basis images determine a plane matrix?
sections.label: Put the images into columns
sections.intro: An input column is a linear combination of the two standard unit columns. Knowing their images determines every output.

blocks.html: The first unit-column image gives the first column of the matrix. The second gives the second column.

blocks.title: Build a matrix from the images of the unit columns
blocks.prompt: The images of \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) are \(\left[\begin{matrix}3\\2\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\-2\end{matrix}\right]\) respectively. Find the image of \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\).
blocks.hint: Images of unit inputs give columns in the matrix, in order.
blocks.solution:
The two supplied images are the first and second columns of the map matrix \(\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1\\2 & -2\end{matrix}\right]\).

The input point is the first unit column multiplied by \(2\) plus the second multiplied by \(1\).

The corresponding combination of image columns is \(\left[\begin{matrix}7\\2\end{matrix}\right]\).

blocks.html: Do not turn the unit images into rows. That generally gives a different map.

sections.title: How can I build a standard transformation without memorising it?
sections.label: Track both unit directions
sections.intro: Use the definition of a rotation or reflection to locate the images of the positive coordinate axes.

blocks.html: A rotation preserves lengths and orientation. A reflection preserves lengths and reverses orientation.

blocks.title: Track both coordinates under a standard plane map
blocks.prompt: Apply a reflection in the line y = x to the point \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\). Enter the image coordinates.
blocks.hint: Visualise where each positive coordinate axis points after the map.
blocks.solution:
Work out the images of the two unit vectors. They are \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\).

Put these in order as columns to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}0 & 1\\1 & 0\end{matrix}\right]\).

The product by the original point gives \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\end{matrix}\right]\).

blocks.html: Check the sign of the rotation by mentally moving the positive x-axis through the given angle.

sections.title: Which factor acts first in a composition?
sections.label: Apply the rightmost matrix first
sections.intro: The input is a column on the far right. The factor closest to it acts first; each subsequent factor acts on the previous image.

blocks.html: If A acts first and B acts second, the composite matrix is \(BA\). Verify with a single test point.

figure.caption: Follow the point from input to shear to stretch in that order.
figure.alt: The point (1, 2) moves to (5, 2) under the shear, then to (10, 2) under the stretch. All three points have the same height.

blocks.title: Apply a shear before a stretch
blocks.prompt: Apply the shear \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 3\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\) and then the stretch \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 0\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the top-right entry of the composition and the image of \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\).
blocks.hint: The rightmost factor acts first when it multiplies a column.
blocks.solution:
The first action touches the input first, so the composition is \(BA\).

Multiplication gives \(\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 9\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Compare with applying the maps to the input one by one.

The image of the point is \(\left[\begin{matrix}15\\1\end{matrix}\right]\).

blocks.html: The chronological order of the written instruction is opposite to the left-to-right order of the factors multiplying a column.

blocks.title: Apply a shear before a stretch
blocks.prompt: Apply the shear \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 5\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\) and then the stretch \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}5 & 0\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the top-right entry of the composition and the image of \(\left[\begin{matrix}4\\-1\end{matrix}\right]\).
blocks.hint: The rightmost factor acts first when it multiplies a column.
blocks.solution:
The first action touches the input first, so the composition is \(BA\).

Multiplication gives \(\left[\begin{matrix}5 & 25\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Compare with applying the maps to the input one by one.

The image of the point is \(\left[\begin{matrix}-5\\-1\end{matrix}\right]\).

sections.title: Can I find a matrix from two non-standard inputs?
sections.label: Solve a matrix equation
sections.intro: Two independent input columns form an invertible matrix X when placed side by side. Put their corresponding images into Y in the same order.

blocks.html: The map matrix satisfies \(AX=Y\), hence \(A=YX^{-1}\).

blocks.title: Recover a transformation from two independent images
blocks.prompt: A map sends \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\end{matrix}\right]\) to \(\left[\begin{matrix}5\\7\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}3\\-1\end{matrix}\right]\) to \(\left[\begin{matrix}8\\-7\end{matrix}\right]\). Find its matrix.
blocks.hint: Only images of the two standard unit inputs are themselves the columns of A.
blocks.solution:
Put the two input columns into matrix \(X\) and the image columns into matrix \(Y\).

The map matrix \(A\) satisfies \(AX=Y\). The input columns are independent, so X is invertible.

Multiply on the right by \(X^{-1}\) to get \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1\\-1 & 4\end{matrix}\right]\).

blocks.html: Two parallel inputs do not determine a general plane matrix. Check independence before inverting.

sections.title: How can I transform an entire straight line?
sections.label: Express old coordinates using new ones
sections.intro: A point on a line satisfies its original equation in the original coordinates. The inverse transformation writes those coordinates in terms of the image coordinates.

blocks.html: Substitute the inverse coordinate formulae into the original equation to obtain the image line. Alternatively transform two distinct points and join their images if they remain distinct.

blocks.title: Substitute the inverse coordinates to transform a line
blocks.prompt: The map uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0\\3 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the gradient and intercept of the image of \(y=2 x + 4\).
blocks.hint: An equation for the image uses new coordinates. Use the inverse map to replace the old ones.
blocks.solution:
The image coordinates satisfy \(x'=x\) and \(y'=3x+y\).

Use the inverse relations \(x=x'\) and \(y=y'-3x'\) in the original line.

The image is \(y'=5x'+4\).

blocks.html: Substituting the forward map directly usually gives the preimage rather than the image.

blocks.title: Substitute the inverse coordinates to transform a line
blocks.prompt: The map uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0\\5 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the gradient and intercept of the image of \(y=4 x + 6\).
blocks.hint: An equation for the image uses new coordinates. Use the inverse map to replace the old ones.
blocks.solution:
The image coordinates satisfy \(x'=x\) and \(y'=5x+y\).

Use the inverse relations \(x=x'\) and \(y=y'-5x'\) in the original line.

The image is \(y'=9x'+6\).

examples.title: Build a matrix from the images of the unit columns
examples.question: The images of \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) are \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\2\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\-1\end{matrix}\right]\) respectively. Find the image of \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\end{matrix}\right]\).
solution: The two supplied images are the first and second columns of the map matrix \(\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 1\\2 & -1\end{matrix}\right]\).
The input point is the first unit column multiplied by \(1\) plus the second multiplied by \(2\).
The corresponding combination of image columns is \(\left[\begin{matrix}4\\0\end{matrix}\right]\).

examples.title: Track both coordinates under a standard plane map
examples.question: Apply a 90° anticlockwise rotation about the origin to the point \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\end{matrix}\right]\). Enter the image coordinates.
solution: Work out the images of the two unit vectors. They are \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}-1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\).
Put these in order as columns to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}0 & -1\\1 & 0\end{matrix}\right]\).
The product by the original point gives \(\left[\begin{matrix}-2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\).

examples.title: Apply a shear before a stretch
examples.question: Apply the shear \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 2\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\) and then the stretch \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 0\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the top-right entry of the composition and the image of \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\end{matrix}\right]\).
solution: The first action touches the input first, so the composition is \(BA\).
Multiplication gives \(\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 4\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Compare with applying the maps to the input one by one.
The image of the point is \(\left[\begin{matrix}10\\2\end{matrix}\right]\).

examples.title: Apply a shear before a stretch
examples.question: Apply the shear \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 4\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\) and then the stretch \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 0\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the top-right entry of the composition and the image of \(\left[\begin{matrix}3\\0\end{matrix}\right]\).
solution: The first action touches the input first, so the composition is \(BA\).
Multiplication gives \(\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 16\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Compare with applying the maps to the input one by one.
The image of the point is \(\left[\begin{matrix}12\\0\end{matrix}\right]\).

examples.title: Recover a transformation from two independent images
examples.question: A map sends \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\end{matrix}\right]\) to \(\left[\begin{matrix}4\\5\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\end{matrix}\right]\) to \(\left[\begin{matrix}3\\-5\end{matrix}\right]\). Find its matrix.
solution: Put the two input columns into matrix \(X\) and the image columns into matrix \(Y\).
The map matrix \(A\) satisfies \(AX=Y\). The input columns are independent, so X is invertible.
Multiply on the right by \(X^{-1}\) to get \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 1\\-1 & 3\end{matrix}\right]\).

examples.title: Substitute the inverse coordinates to transform a line
examples.question: The map uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0\\2 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the gradient and intercept of the image of \(y=x + 3\).
solution: The image coordinates satisfy \(x'=x\) and \(y'=2x+y\).
Use the inverse relations \(x=x'\) and \(y=y'-2x'\) in the original line.
The image is \(y'=3x'+3\).

examples.title: Substitute the inverse coordinates to transform a line
examples.question: The map uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0\\4 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the gradient and intercept of the image of \(y=3 x + 5\).
solution: The image coordinates satisfy \(x'=x\) and \(y'=4x+y\).
Use the inverse relations \(x=x'\) and \(y=y'-4x'\) in the original line.
The image is \(y'=7x'+5\).

extraPractice.title: Build a matrix from the images of the unit columns
extraPractice.prompt: The images of \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) are \(\left[\begin{matrix}4\\2\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\-3\end{matrix}\right]\) respectively. Find the image of \(\left[\begin{matrix}3\\0\end{matrix}\right]\).
extraPractice.hint: Images of unit inputs give columns in the matrix, in order.
extraPractice.solution:
The two supplied images are the first and second columns of the map matrix \(\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 1\\2 & -3\end{matrix}\right]\).

The input point is the first unit column multiplied by \(3\) plus the second multiplied by \(0\).

The corresponding combination of image columns is \(\left[\begin{matrix}12\\6\end{matrix}\right]\).

extraPractice.title: Track both coordinates under a standard plane map

extraPractice.solution:
Work out the images of the two unit vectors. They are \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}-1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\).

Put these in order as columns to obtain \(\left[\begin{matrix}0 & -1\\1 & 0\end{matrix}\right]\).

The product by the original point gives \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\3\end{matrix}\right]\).

extraPractice.prompt: Apply the shear \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 6\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\) and then the stretch \(B=\left[\begin{matrix}6 & 0\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the top-right entry of the composition and the image of \(\left[\begin{matrix}5\\-2\end{matrix}\right]\).
extraPractice.hint: The rightmost factor acts first when it multiplies a column.
extraPractice.solution:
The first action touches the input first, so the composition is \(BA\).

Multiplication gives \(\left[\begin{matrix}6 & 36\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Compare with applying the maps to the input one by one.

The image of the point is \(\left[\begin{matrix}-42\\-2\end{matrix}\right]\).

extraPractice.title: Recover a transformation from two independent images
extraPractice.prompt: A map sends \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\end{matrix}\right]\) to \(\left[\begin{matrix}6\\9\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}4\\-1\end{matrix}\right]\) to \(\left[\begin{matrix}15\\-9\end{matrix}\right]\). Find its matrix.
extraPractice.hint: Only images of the two standard unit inputs are themselves the columns of A.
extraPractice.solution:
Put the two input columns into matrix \(X\) and the image columns into matrix \(Y\).

The map matrix \(A\) satisfies \(AX=Y\). The input columns are independent, so X is invertible.

Multiply on the right by \(X^{-1}\) to get \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 1\\-1 & 5\end{matrix}\right]\).

extraPractice.title: Substitute the inverse coordinates to transform a line
extraPractice.prompt: The map uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0\\6 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the gradient and intercept of the image of \(y=5 x + 7\).
extraPractice.hint: An equation for the image uses new coordinates. Use the inverse map to replace the old ones.
extraPractice.solution:
The image coordinates satisfy \(x'=x\) and \(y'=6x+y\).

Use the inverse relations \(x=x'\) and \(y=y'-6x'\) in the original line.

The image is \(y'=11x'+7\).

sections.title: How do I find all points that stay exactly where they are?
sections.label: Solve a fixed-point equation
sections.intro: A fixed point has its original coordinates after applying the map. Set the image equal to the original coordinate column.

blocks.html: Solve \((A-I)\mathbf v=\mathbf0\). A free variable can describe an entire fixed line.

blocks.title: Find fixed points by solving the two coordinate equations
blocks.prompt: For \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 3\\0 & -1\end{matrix}\right]\), which axis consists entirely of fixed points? Give the other coordinate shared by every fixed point.

fields.label: Value of y at a fixed point

blocks.hint: Solve Av = v, which is stronger than requiring the image to remain on its original line.
blocks.solution:
Set the image column equal to the original one. This gives \(3y=0\) and \(-y=y\).

Hence \(y=0\) and x is unrestricted.

Every point on the x-axis is fixed. A point off that axis changes its y-coordinate.

blocks.html: The origin is fixed by every linear transformation, but it need not be the only fixed point.

sections.title: Can a line be invariant even while points move along it?
sections.label: Distinguish equality of sets from equality of points
sections.intro: A line is invariant if it is mapped onto itself. Individual points can move to different positions on the same line.

blocks.html: For a line through the origin, a non-zero image parallel to a direction vector is enough to preserve it as a line.

blocks.title: Distinguish an invariant line from a line of fixed points
blocks.prompt: The transformation uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 0\\0 & 4\end{matrix}\right]\). Give the multiplier on the y-axis, and decide whether the whole y-axis is fixed point by point.
blocks.hint: A line can map onto itself even if particular positions on it change.
blocks.solution:
A point of the y-axis has x-coordinate zero. Applying A leaves that coordinate zero and multiplies y by \(4\).

The output remains on the axis, so the line is invariant.

The multiplier is not one. Except for the origin, the points move along the line.

blocks.html: A zero image of its direction collapses the whole line to a point. That does not map the line onto itself.

sections.title: How do I test a line that does not pass through the origin?
sections.label: Use a general point with the offset
sections.intro: An affine line has a direction and an offset. Preserving the direction alone does not guarantee that the line stays where it was.

blocks.html: Check that a general image point obeys the original line equation and that the direction is not collapsed.

figure.caption: A shear can preserve a line without fixing the points on it.
figure.alt: The point (1, 2) moves along the horizontal line to (5, 2). The line stays the same even though the point moves.

blocks.title: Check a horizontal line that misses the origin
blocks.prompt: The shear uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 3\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Decide whether the line \(y=3\) is invariant and find the x-coordinate of the image of \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\3\end{matrix}\right]\).
blocks.hint: To check an affine line, test a general point on it and account for its offset from the origin.
blocks.solution:
The matrix leaves every y-coordinate unchanged. The image of every point on the horizontal line stays on that line.

The inverse shear also keeps the same line, so the line maps onto itself.

The x-coordinate changes to \(10\) for the given point.

blocks.html: Do not check only the point chosen for convenience. Verify the whole line stays invariant.

blocks.title: Check a horizontal line that misses the origin
blocks.prompt: The shear uses \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 5\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\). Decide whether the line \(y=5\) is invariant and find the x-coordinate of the image of \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\5\end{matrix}\right]\).
blocks.hint: To check an affine line, test a general point on it and account for its offset from the origin.
blocks.solution:

The x-coordinate changes to \(26\) for the given point.

sections.title: Why should I check the vertical line separately?
sections.label: Solve for finite slopes, then use the vertical direction
sections.intro: The direction vector with first entry one represents every finite slope. No finite slope represents a vertical line.

blocks.html: For finite slope m, require the image of the column with entries one and m to be parallel to that column. Test the vertical unit direction separately.

blocks.title: Find finite invariant slopes and check the vertical axis
blocks.prompt: Find the slopes of all invariant lines through the origin for \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}5 & 1\\6 & 4\end{matrix}\right]\). Is the vertical line through the origin invariant?
blocks.hint: Test the vertical direction independently of the finite-slope equation.
blocks.solution:
A finite slope \(m\) has a direction column \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\m\end{matrix}\right]\). The image must be parallel to it.

Equating cross products of the coordinates gives \(m^{2} + m - 6=0\), with the two slopes \(2\) and \(-3\).

The image of the vertical direction is \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\4\end{matrix}\right]\). Its first coordinate is non-zero, so the vertical line is not invariant.

blocks.html: An equation for finite slopes cannot rule out an additional vertical invariant line.

sections.title: Which coordinates change in a spatial map?
sections.label: Read the axis or plane of the map
sections.intro: A rotation about a coordinate axis leaves its coordinate unchanged and rotates the two perpendicular coordinates. A reflection in a coordinate plane reverses the perpendicular coordinate.

blocks.html: Build the three-dimensional matrix from the three unit images. Track their order and the given direction of rotation.

blocks.title: Read a three-coordinate transformation along an axis or plane
blocks.prompt: Find the image of \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\1\\6\end{matrix}\right]\) under reflection in the xz-plane.
blocks.hint: Identify the unaffected coordinate before changing the others.
blocks.solution:
Use a two-coordinate rule on the affected axes. The x and z positions stay fixed while y changes sign.

The three unit images give the matrix \(\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0\\0 & -1 & 0\\0 & 0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\).

Its product with the given column is \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\6\end{matrix}\right]\).

blocks.html: The unaffected coordinate should appear unchanged. Do not reverse the orientation of the rotation when changing axes.

blocks.title: Read a three-coordinate transformation along an axis or plane
